trace.claim: The paper asks how regional political climate moderates the association between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
Political climate moderates the conservatism-vaccine hesitancy association, with conservatives in liberal climates being less hesitant than conservatives in conservative regions.
The study uses online self-reported survey data from 683 U.S. participants collected March 8 to April 19 2023.
There is a significant interaction between political conservatism and conservative political climate for vaccine and booster hesitancy.
Liberals are less likely to be vaccine hesitant regardless of political climate.
The interaction also holds for booster uptake likelihood.
Conservatives’ booster uptake is associated with their political climate while liberals’ uptake is not.
The authors note the data are cross-sectional so causal or directional associations cannot be assumed.
Self-reported vaccine status is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias.
The authors situate the work in an emerging evidence base that broader political climate can influence COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
Previous research has identified separate effects of political orientation and political climate but little work on their interaction.
